analysis.one_liner: Requires large federal contractors to disclose labor violations, show workers their pay, and limit forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 Democratic senators and no Republicans, died in the Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would use the government's buying power to improve working conditions at companies with big federal contracts. Any company bidding for a federal contract worth more than $500,000 would have to disclose whether it was found to have violated wage, safety, discrimination, or other labor laws in the past three years, and agencies could weigh that record when deciding who wins the contract. It would also require contractors to give workers a plain record of their hours and pay each pay period, tell independent contractors they are not employees, and stop contractors from forcing workers into arbitration for sexual harassment or discrimination claims unless the worker agreed after the dispute arose. It would revive an Obama-era rule that Congress voted to cancel in 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly hundreds of thousands of people who work for companies that hold large federal contracts. They would get an itemized record of hours and pay each pay period, notice if they are being treated as an independent contractor, and protection against being forced into secret arbitration over sexual harassment or discrimination claims. Responsible employers would also benefit, because a single reporting website would consolidate contract reporting requirements.

how_it_helps.text: Companies bidding for contracts over $500,000 would have to disclose labor-law violations from the past three years, and every six months during the contract, so agencies could weigh the record before awarding work.

Contractors would have to give covered workers a pay-period document showing hours worked, overtime, pay, and any additions to or deductions from pay, and tell independent contractors they are not employees.
Federal contracts could not require workers to arbitrate sexual harassment or discrimination claims unless the worker voluntarily agreed after the dispute arose.
Federal funds could not be spent on activities aimed at persuading employees for or against unionizing.
The bill would reissue the 2016 Fair Pay and Safe Workplaces rule that Congress voted to cancel in 2017, and establish one website for all federal contractor reporting requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and their subcontractors, in construction, defense, and services, would bear the cost of tracking and reporting labor-law compliance, pay records, and arbitration terms, and companies with violation records would risk losing contracts or being referred for suspension. Some of that cost would be built into contract bids paid by taxpayers, and the 2016 version of the rule drew lawsuits from contractors who said its disclosure requirements were unfair and unworkable.

drawbacks.text: Contractors would face new reporting and compliance duties on every contract and subcontract over $500,000, with updates every six months, costs that would partly be passed through to the government in bids.

The disclosure requirement covers any administrative decision, arbitration award, or civil judgment over a long list of labor laws, and the earlier version of this rule was challenged in court by contractors who argued it could disqualify companies over disputed or minor allegations; the bill's defenders point to its corrective-measure provisions, which give agencies discretion to weigh remediation rather than penalize automatically.

The arbitration protection does not cover workers under a collective bargaining agreement or workers who signed an arbitration agreement before their employer bid on the contract, so many union workers and some newly hired workers would not get it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are concrete and aimed at real, documented problems: wage theft and safety violations by federal contractors, and mandatory arbitration clauses that bury harassment claims. The main honest cost is compliance paperwork for contractors, which the bill tries to reduce with a single reporting website and discretion for agencies to weigh corrective action. The design choice to exempt unionized workers from the arbitration protection is a real gap. On balance, the gains to workers on large federal contracts outweigh the reporting burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on March 11, 2020, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it.
No vote was ever held in the Senate or House before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
A key purpose of the bill was to reissue the Obama-era 2016 rule by statute, which would get around Public Law 115-11, the 2017 law that canceled that rule.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors are better off: no new disclosure obligations, no risk of losing bids over labor-violation records, and forced arbitration clauses covering harassment claims remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractors, whose status quo held

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought the original Senate sponsors on board.

for.name: 10 Democratic Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (Blumenthal, Brown, Baldwin, Feinstein, Murray, Gillibrand, Van Hollen, Shaheen, Merkley, Durbin)

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill out after it was referred.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill; a labor-law bill backed only by Democrats was unlikely to get committee time under Republican leadership.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; as the member who controls what gets scheduled, no vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee in a Republican-led Senate.

industries.industry: Federal contractors (construction, defense, and professional services)
industries.note: These companies would have to disclose labor-law violations on bids worth over $500,000, keep pay-transparency records, and drop mandatory arbitration for harassment claims. Their interest in the bill runs against workers, since the disclosure rules put contract revenue at risk for companies with violation records.

industries.industry: Staffing and temp agencies relying on independent-contractor classification
industries.note: The bill requires companies to tell workers classified as independent contractors that they are not employees, increasing exposure to misclassification disputes on federal work.

industries.industry: Employer-side law firms and union-avoidance consultants
industries.note: Federal funds could no longer be spent on consultants or legal counsel used to persuade employees against unionizing on covered contracts.
